chunks: Ambient light effects on cameras. The question: How does ambient lighting impact camera performance?
The light in a scene changes a camera's picture in three ways: how much light there is, what color it is, and how steady it is. Too little light gives grain and blur.
Tinted light makes colors look wrong. Flickering light makes bands in the image.
Your own eyes do the same. In a dim room you struggle to see fine detail. Under a yellow bulb a white sheet looks yellow until your brain adjusts.
Under a flickering tube light you see a faint strobing. Your brain fixes much of this; a camera must calculate each fix.
The eye picture hides one thing: a camera also has a limit on how much contrast it can capture in one shot.
The 1/30 seconds curve is about 1. 02 electrons per lux (order of magnitude, spectrum-dependent).
At the typical office 500 lux the pixel is comfortably in shot-noise territory (27 decibels); at 5 lux it's barely above 0 decibels.
Shortening the exposure to 1/250 seconds to freeze motion costs 8.
3x less light: about 9 decibels of SNR where shot noise dominates, and up to 18 decibels at the read-noise-limited dark end; that's the trade-off between blur and noise.
Lux: a brightness unit based on what the human eye sees. Color temperature: how warm or cool a light looks. A candle-like bulb is warm, near 2700 K.
Daylight is cooler, near 6500 K. White balance: adjusting red, green and blue so that white objects look white under that light.
Flicker: brightness that pulses rapidly, such as 100 times a second on 50 hertz wall power (as in Europe).
Dynamic range: the span from darkest to brightest detail a camera can capture in one shot.
An office is about 500 lux. A night street is about 5 lux, so 100 times darker.
A small phone pixel might collect about 510 electrons in 1/30 seconds at the office, and only about 5 on the street. The grain is about the square root of the count.
That gives a signal-to-noise ratio of about 23 at the office and about 2 on the street.
Now flicker: on 50 hertz power the lamp pulses 100 times a second, so each pulse lasts 10 milliseconds.
An exposure of 1/100 seconds covers exactly one flicker, and the bands vanish.
"Light affects a camera three ways.
Level: signal scales with lux, shot noise means SNR goes as root signal, so dim scenes need longer exposures or more gain and get noisy or blurry, and autofocus struggles.
Spectrum: different lights shift raw color, so white balance has to estimate the illuminant, and LED spectra can cause color errors.
And time structure: mains and PWM lights flicker, which causes banding unless exposure is matched. High contrast scenes also exceed dynamic range, so you need HDR."
